index.label: Do it, be it, do it

brief.head: Nobody’s watching
brief.text: The deep­est anx­i­ety is what oth­ers think, Amit Varma said, and it took him till mid­dle age to see that no one is think­ing of you. {011-C11}

brief.head: We are all stupid
brief.text: Each of us knows a hand­ful of things well, Varma ar­gued. In ev­ery­thing else we are stupid, so be hum­ble, and don’t judge oth­ers. {011-C12}

brief.head: Your edge is you
brief.text: Chase trends or the al­go­rithm and you lose your unique­ness, Varma said. “The only thing that sep­a­rates me from the 8 bil­lion peo­ple on this planet is me.” {011-C04}

brief.head: Shelling pine nuts
brief.text: Ghazala Wahab’s grand­fa­ther is not called lov­ing: he shells pine nuts all day to re­ward the chil­dren. That, Varma said, is show­ing, not telling. {011-C08}

brief.head: Small tools, big jobs
brief.text: Unix is a way of think­ing, not just a tool, Ajay Shah said: many small tools, strung to­gether to per­form any task. {011-C20}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: The prob­lem with prac­ti­cal goals is that you’ll ac­tu­ally achieve them.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that purpose, not talent or targets, keeps people running

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on getting things done
lead.head: All the world’s a vegetable

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 11

body: Ajay Shah opened with a fore­cast for the mer­chan­dis­ing trade: the slo­gan “just do it” was about to be over­pow­ered by a new one, “Kaator re bhaaji”. Both hosts were wear­ing it on their t-shirts. {011-J01}
The words are Konkani. Over the next hour, Amit Varma un­packed them into rules for get­ting work done, and Shah steered the talk to­wards pur­pose.

The mantra comes from a story Jerry Pinto told Varma on *The Seen and the Unseen*. Abbé Faria, a Goan child prodigy born in 1756, was in­vited as a teenager to speak be­fore the Queen of Portugal in Lisbon. On stage, fac­ing the queen, the roy­alty and his own fa­ther, he froze.
His fa­ther leaned for­ward and hissed at him. In Varma’s ren­der­ing: “All these are veg­eta­bles. Cut the veg­eta­bles, cut the veg­eta­bles, cut the veg­eta­bles.” {011-C01}
Whatever we do in our lives, Varma said, “it boils down to cut­ting the veg­eta­bles, to build­ing a habit, to rou­tine”.
## Four slo­gans, two U-turns
Varma then of­fered four slo­gans, each pulling against the one be­fore. The first was Nike’s: just do it. You get some­thing right, he said, by get­ting it done again and again. {011-C02}

Shah tem­pered it. Repetition helps only if you can sense the gra­di­ent of the hill you are climb­ing. “It is pos­si­ble to just keep doing the same thing over and over and being bad at it every sin­gle time,” he said.
Invited to con­tra­dict him­self, Varma of­fered the sec­ond slo­gan: don’t do it, just be it. Decide who the best ver­sion of you is, he said, and let the habits flow from that self-image.
The third re­versed the sec­ond: don’t be it, just do it. Praise chil­dren for their ef­fort, not their in­tel­li­gence. Verbs mat­ter; ad­jec­tives don’t.

The fourth gath­ered up the rest: habits are ev­ery­thing. Ask a hun­dred writ­ers about their goals and you can­not tell the good from the bad. Ask about their habits, Varma said, “and you will never be wrong”.
Shah’s method is to take on one habit at a time, for two or three months of focus, until it runs on au­topi­lot. Six at once, he said, can­not be done.
## From tools to pur­pose
Varma demon­strated Roam Research, the note-taking tool he uses to pre­pare his episodes, and ar­gued that the form of our input and out­put shapes how we think.
Shah’s choice was older. After 40 years around com­put­ers, he said, Unix and the com­mand line re­main the most pro­duc­tive and pow­er­ful en­vi­ron­ment there is. {011-R15}
Asked to zoom out, Shah set pro­duc­tiv­ity aside for pur­pose. Practical goals are weak fuel, he ar­gued, be­cause once you reach them you are left ask­ing what comes next.
Life or­gan­ised around sta­tus mark­ers, from the fa­mous uni­ver­sity to the top jour­nal, is a poor op­er­at­ing sys­tem, he said, be­cause it does not har­ness the mind. {011-C15}
The real su­per­pow­ers, in his telling, are cu­rios­ity and en­durance, put to work for a pur­pose.

Shah did not claim his tech­nique was the right one. But each of us, he said, has to ask why we are here, and find “that marathon runner’s abil­ity to run long, dif­fi­cult jour­neys with­out the sim­ple grat­i­fi­ca­tion of ex­ter­nal val­i­da­tion”.

second.label: What talent is
second.head: Talent, rain or shine
second.deck: Amit Varma recalls a sportsman whose gift was getting up anyway

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the athlete who ran in the rain

body: A top sportsper­son, asked about his great­est tal­ent, gave an an­swer Amit Varma read in the early 2000s and still talks about. It sounded very Dravid-esque, Varma said, but it was not Rahul Dravid, and he has failed to track it down. {#dravidesque}

The ath­lete ran every day at five. Suppose he woke with a cold, his goal for the year al­ready met, a hol­i­day com­ing and rain out­side. He would still get up and run. That, he said, was tal­ent. {011-S06}
We think of tal­ent as nat­u­ral ge­nius, Varma said. Sometimes it is just the qual­ity “which makes you dogged, which makes you go out there and do it and just get the job done”. {#dogged}

quote.text: I will still get up and go run­ning in the rain. That’s tal­ent.

third.head: The pot thickens

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the pottery experiment

body: A group of peo­ple was split into two halves, Amit Varma said. One half had a week to make a sin­gle pot, and could spend the week re­search­ing and plan­ning it. The other was told to make as many pots as they wanted. {011-S02}
The plan­ners read books and worked out in the­ory what makes a per­fect pot. Varma pic­tured them tak­ing on­line cour­ses in “the art of clear pot­tery”, a nod to his own writ­ing course. {011-J05}
The sec­ond group sim­ply got the job done, again and again. The best pots came from them.
Ajay Shah added a cau­tion. Iteration needs a sense of which way is up­hill, he said; with­out one, peo­ple can stay bad for­ever. {011-C05}

p2.title: Do it, be it, do it
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s four slogans for getting things done, and Ajay Shah’s case for purpose over productivity

quote.text: You get some­thing right by get­ting it done again and again and again.

box.title: The man behind the mantra
box.text: Abbé Faria, born José Custódio de Faria in Candolim in 1756, left India after a re­bel­lion, took part in the French Revolution and be­came one of the fa­thers of hyp­no­tism. Alexandre Dumas named a char­ac­ter in *The Count of Monte Cristo* after him. {011-R22}

sections.label: The first slogan
sections.head: Get it done, then get it right
sections.caption: getting it done before getting it right
body: Every ven­ture, Amit Varma said, in­volves a trade-off be­tween get­ting it done and get­ting it right. He has a bias to­wards get­ting it done. {011-C02}
For a writer, the first draft is where you get it done: “Take a dump of the brain.” Rodin, he said, did not fash­ion *The Thinker* out of thin air. He took a block of stone and edited it. {011-J11}
His friend Vinay Sitapati put it an­other way: “Never let per­fec­tion be the enemy of pro­duc­tion.”

The YouTuber Ali Abdaal needed half a year of two videos a week to reach his 50th video and his first thou­sand sub­scribers. Everyone sucks at the start, Varma said, so any­one driven by val­i­da­tion stops be­fore get­ting good. {011-C03}
## Standards and mo­men­tum

Ajay Shah agreed, then tem­pered it. Iteration needs a sense of the gra­di­ent of the hill you are climb­ing. India cel­e­brates *jugaad*, he said, which to him is “just a fancy name given for peo­ple who do things re­ally badly”. {011-C05}
His role in India, he said, has been to push stan­dards: “No, this ain’t good enough. Can we try harder?” But no­body should be paral­ysed by per­fec­tion­ism.

~ Varma’s own ap­pren­tice­ship was his blog, India Uncut, from around 2003-04: five posts a day, about 8,000 in five years. “There was no anx­i­ety about get­ting it per­fect,” he said. “It was me think­ing aloud.”

quote.text: You get some­thing right by get­ting it done again and again and again.

sections.label: The second slogan
sections.head: A reader, not a timetable
sections.caption: being the best version of yourself
body: Told by Ajay Shah to con­tra­dict him­self, Amit Varma obliged, “for we con­tain mul­ti­tudes, as the great Walt Whitman once said”. {011-J09} His sec­ond slo­gan: don’t do it, just be it.

Most of us build a habit by timetable, he said: read every evening from seven to eight. Day one goes well, and day two. By day three you fall off the wagon, and by day four some­body is wrong on the in­ter­net and you have to cor­rect them. {011-J06}
Then the dam­age spreads to your self-image. You de­cide you are not a reader, per­haps a Netflix kind of per­son, and the game is over.

Instead, pic­ture the best ver­sion of your­self: a self-taught poly­math who, when bored, picks up a book and not the phone. Own that iden­tity, Varma said, and the habits flow from it. Miss a day and it means noth­ing. {011-C06}
## The image prob­lem

Shah asked about the image we show the world: it can keep us ac­count­able, or breed im­poster syn­drome. Varma’s an­swer was that it took him into mid­dle age to re­alise that no one is think­ing of you. No one, he said, is tak­ing screen­shots to shame you on Twitter, “or ac­tu­ally in my case, they are”. {011-J08}
~ Social media makes things worse, he ar­gued, by set­ting our real selves against the pro­jected selves of oth­ers.

quote.text: Where your self-image drives your habits and not the other way around.

portraits.caption: Walt Whitman
portraits.credit: George Collins Cox / Adam Cuerden, public domain

sections.label: The third slogan
sections.head: Verbs matter, adjectives don’t
sections.caption: praising effort, not cleverness
body: The third slo­gan undid the sec­ond: don’t be it, just do it. Amit Varma took it from a study by Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck, which he found through an episode of the *Huberman Lab* pod­cast. {011-R07}

Children given a com­mon task were split in two. One half was praised for at­tributes: you’re so in­tel­li­gent. The other half was praised for ef­fort. The first group did worse in later tests, and some might even cheat. The sec­ond kept doing well. {011-C07}

Varma looks back on his own life with “a touch of re­gret and sad­ness”. Things came eas­ily to him: an exam oth­ers stud­ied 20 hours for, he could do in 20 min­utes. “And this is a great trap,” he said. {011-S07}
## A num­ber on the fore­head

Ajay Shah, by his own ac­count the lucky child who blos­somed at the right age, called India’s early la­belling of chil­dren as smart or dumb “a truly toxic thing”. Everybody, he said, started paint­ing a num­ber on his fore­head. {011-S08}
Age-sorted class­rooms, he ar­gued, are an in­dus­trial-revolution idea. People who work in ed­u­ca­tion know that dif­fer­ent peo­ple blos­som dif­fer­ently, with no fixed age. {011-C13}
~ Talent, Shah said, is “one of the most harm­ful words”. The two su­per­pow­ers are cu­rios­ity and en­durance.

quote.text: Humans are un­ruly, un­pre­dictable crea­tures and we all blos­som in dif­fer­ent di­men­sions at dif­fer­ent rates.

sections.label: The fourth slogan
sections.head: Two hundred words a day
sections.caption: habits as compound interest
body: The last slo­gan gath­ered up the rest: habits are ev­ery­thing. Amit Varma bor­rowed a line from James Clear’s *Atomic Habits*: “Habits are the com­pound in­ter­est of self-improvement.” {#compound}

His thought ex­per­i­ment comes from his writ­ing class. Gather a hun­dred writ­ers, from great to bad, and ask about their goals: you can­not tell them apart. Ask about their pro­cesses and habits, and you will know who will make it. {011-C09}

Targets must sur­vive a busy life. Writers who set them­selves a thou­sand words a day, and then fail, slide into a *mujhse nahi hoga* spi­ral. Varma asks for 200, about what he speaks in a minute: his speak­ing speed, he said, is 160 to 170 words a minute. {#speed}
A gym mem­ber­ship builds no mus­cle, he added. Going to the gym does.
## One at a time

Ajay Shah linked it to the glu­cose mon­i­tor the hosts had dis­cussed. Watching every meal is a heavy cog­ni­tive bur­den, he said, but a habit takes about two or three months of focus, after which it runs on au­topi­lot. {011-C10}
Asked which habit he was glad he had built, Shah said he had or­gan­ised his whole life around one pur­pose: more hours each day to read. {011-S09}
~ He keeps push­ing away mun­dane things and de­ci­sions, he said, to re­duce the bur­den of ev­ery­day life.

quote.text: You have to fight one thing at a time and it is solv­able.

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: A second brain, with links
sections.caption: Roam Research and the second brain
body: Ajay Shah asked whether the world of pro­duc­tiv­ity tools mat­ters at all. He dis­likes the word it­self: “It’s too much of a man­age­rial thing. It’s too much Taylorism for me.” {011-J15}

Amit Varma an­swered with a demon­stra­tion of Roam Research, the note-taking tool he uses to pre­pare his episodes. Its nested en­tries re­placed the 40-page Word files he once scrolled through madly.

His notes on Ghazala Wahab’s *Born a Muslim* fol­low the book chap­ter by chap­ter. Shah’s notes for their Ukraine episode had de­tailed chap­ters, links and, “like a good aca­demic”, a list of sources. That, Varma said, came from a lifetime’s habit of read­ing. {011-S10}
## The shape of thought
The form of our input and out­put mat­ters, Varma ar­gued. A day with a phys­i­cal book sets one rhythm of mind; a day of scrolling and swip­ing sets a chop­pier one. {011-C17}
His friend Gautam John once looked at his smart­phone, for any­thing other than calls, only be­tween five and six in the evening. {011-S11}
The brain, Varma said, is a messy, im­pres­sion­is­tic ma­chine, which is why he likes Tiago Forte’s idea of a sec­ond brain. {011-C18}

~ Shah put in a word for two al­ter­na­tives. Obsidian, which Varma noted is free, keeps notes as plain Markdown files; Org Mode in Emacs is very pow­er­ful, though it lacks a net­worked, shared ver­sion.

quote.text: All day we are tak­ing in learn­ings that we do not re­tain.

art.caption: Amit Varma on Roam Research and the second brain

sections.label: Ajay zooms out
sections.head: Credentials don’t run a life
sections.caption: purpose, curiosity and endurance
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to zoom out from tac­tics and say how he thinks one should live.

Many of us start out chas­ing sim­ple things: an exam, a job, some money, or “the Louis Vuitton bag of the cre­den­tials”, the fa­mous uni­ver­sity, the fa­mous jour­nal, the fes­ti­val book talk. That, Shah said, is a poor op­er­at­ing sys­tem, be­cause it does not har­ness the mind. {011-C15}
He re­called a talk at which Rahul Dravid said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar, and only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid he could be. {011-S12}
## Thirty years, one year
In re­search, Shah said, “jour­nal ori­en­ta­tion” is toxic ad­vice be­cause it switches off cu­rios­ity.

Years alone do not build ex­pe­ri­ence, he ar­gued. Write an eleventh paper like the first ten and no new ground is bro­ken. What makes a year count is cu­rios­ity, en­durance and a will­ing­ness to chal­lenge the sta­tus quo. {011-C16}
His own jour­ney, he said, has been the fall­ing away of dis­trac­tions, so that he stays con­nected to the core. In some weird way, he has been the same since he was a teenager.
~ Ever since the Greeks, Shah said, we have known that mean­ing comes from being part of some­thing big­ger than one­self. Simple ob­jec­tives har­ness only ten per cent of each of us. {#tenpercent}

quote.text: It’s a poor op­er­at­ing sys­tem, most im­por­tantly, be­cause it ac­tu­ally does not har­ness the mind.
You could be doing thirty years of the same thing over and over, and you’ve ac­tu­ally not been on a life jour­ney of grow­ing and be­com­ing a big­ger and bet­ter and more in­ter­est­ing per­son.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A prodigy, a delay, a prize and a finished program

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Jerry Pinto’s story of a Goan prodigy
stories.head: The boy who froze before a queen
body: José Custódio de Faria was born in 1756 in Candolim, when Goa was a Portuguese colony. His fa­ther was a priest and his mother a nun. They joined the church after hav­ing him, Amit Varma ex­plained, and sep­a­rated.
Ajay Shah placed it be­fore the Battle of Plassey. “There you go,” said Varma. {011-J04}

His fa­ther treated him as a prodigy and took him around to be ed­u­cated. By his teens the boy was fa­mous for his bril­liant ser­mons, and the Queen of Portugal in­vited him to speak in Lisbon, then, Shah noted, one of the great cities of the world.
Varma set the scene with rel­ish: the queen in her green silk emer­ald dress, and all the roy­alty of Lisbon “in their breeches and their gowns, with mag­nif­i­cent smiles and frowns”. {011-J03}
On the stage, with ev­ery­one who mat­tered to him star­ing out of the dark­ness, the boy froze. No words came.
His fa­ther leaned for­ward and hissed in Konkani: *kaator re bhaaji*. All these are veg­eta­bles, Varma trans­lated. Cut the veg­eta­bles. {011-C01}

Faria’s ad­ven­tures did not end there. Caught up in a re­bel­lion, he had to leave India. He took part in the French Revolution and was im­pris­oned, alone, on an is­land. There he re­mem­bered his father’s words, built a men­tal frame­work and be­came one of the fa­thers of hyp­no­tism.
~ In *The Count of Monte Cristo*, Varma added, Alexandre Dumas named a char­ac­ter after him.
stories.why: Big, fright­en­ing mo­ments shrink when you treat them as a pile of veg­eta­bles to chop. Whatever we do in our lives, Varma said, comes down to cut­ting the veg­eta­bles: to habit and rou­tine. {011-S01}
stories.postscript: The hosts wore the mantra on t-shirts made by Varma’s friend Narendra Shenoy. {011-J01}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the whisper in Lisbon

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma disagree about their own show
stories.head: Sharpening an axe, or not
body: By August 2022, in Udaipur, Ajay Shah and Amit Varma were sure they would make this show, and were de­bat­ing names for it. The first episode ar­rived more than a year later.
Shah put the delay down to am­bi­tion. They had “dreams of qual­ity and per­fec­tion­ism”, he said, and a messy, ju­gaad-style start did not meet the bar. {011-S04}

Varma pushed back. Abraham Lincoln, he said, would spend five of six hours sharp­en­ing the axe be­fore chop­ping a tree. {#lincoln} But the hosts had not been sharp­en­ing any­thing. Varma had sim­ply been pro­cras­ti­nat­ing.

~ What fi­nally got it mov­ing was a chance brain­storm with a pro­ducer friend, Vartika: she was a pro­fes­sional, they could get her to do it, and once it had mo­men­tum they could fig­ure out the rest.
stories.why: It is easy to pass off pro­cras­ti­na­tion as prepa­ra­tion. You need stan­dards and mo­men­tum both, and the hosts dis­agree on the bal­ance: Varma still says they should have started when they con­ceived the show. {#started}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the year before Episode One

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the Nobel question he asks friends
stories.head: Not playing the Nobel game
body: Amit Varma some­times asks peo­ple in his cir­cles a ques­tion: of all the guests on *The Seen and the Unseen*, who is most likely to win a Nobel Prize? The stan­dard an­swer is the econ­o­mist Karthik Muralidharan, who, Varma said, is clearly on that track.

Varma’s own rule is to name the most bril­liant per­son he knows. On his show, at the risk of em­bar­rass­ing him, that was Ajay Shah. When Varma told him so, Shah said he was not on that track. {#track}
With great sad­ness, Varma agreed. Shah, he said, had de­fined his pur­pose dif­fer­ently and was play­ing a dif­fer­ent kind of game. {011-S13}
~ People who do play that game, like Muralidharan, are doing amaz­ing work, Varma said, and more power to them.
stories.why: Prizes re­ward those who play a par­tic­u­lar game. Someone who has de­fined his pur­pose dif­fer­ently, Varma sug­gested, can be bril­liant and still choose not to play it. Shah, by his own ac­count, is not on that track.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Nobel Prize question

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s tribute to a program that is finished
stories.head: A Taj Mahal made of code
body: Hidden in­side the Unix toolchain, Ajay Shah said, is TeX, a pro­fes­sional type­set­ting sys­tem used by many pub­lish­ers. Many of the great books of the world are set with it. {011-R16}

Its main au­thor, Donald Knuth, is one of the world’s great thinkers and spent his whole life pol­ish­ing it. Now that he is old, he says TeX is fin­ished: it needs no fur­ther fea­ture, and it has no recorded bugs. {#finished}
The code is open, and any­one may build on it. Knuth asks only that after he is gone, they call it some­thing else. “This is my Taj Mahal,” he says. “I built this.” {011-S14}
~ When a bug does turn up, Knuth writes the finder a cheque. The find­ers frame it and hang it on their walls.
stories.why: TeX shows that a pro­gram can ac­tu­ally be fin­ished, and gives, Shah said, a flavour of the ma­tu­rity of Unix. Most soft­ware, by con­trast, is “just some rub­bish lay­ered on rub­bish”. {011-C19}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Donald Knuth’s TeX

quiz.q: What did Abbé Faria’s father hiss at him in Lisbon, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: “Kaator re bhaaji”: Konkani for “all these are veg­eta­bles, cut the veg­eta­bles”.

quiz.q: In the pottery experiment Amit Varma described, which group made the best pots?
quiz.a: The group told to make as many pots as they liked.

quiz.q: What did Ali Abdaal advise new YouTubers to do before looking at their metrics?
quiz.a: Make two videos a week for two years: about 200 videos.

quiz.q: What did the study by Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck find about praising children?
quiz.a: Children praised for in­tel­li­gence did worse; those praised for ef­fort kept im­prov­ing.

quiz.q: Which Indian cricketer said he only tried to be the best version of himself?
quiz.a: Rahul Dravid, who said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar.

quiz.q: Around what single purpose has Ajay Shah organised his whole life?
quiz.a: Getting more hours each day to read, by cut­ting mun­dane tasks.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 11. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Donald Knuth (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5); Auguste Rodin (Nadar, public domain); Walt Whitman (George Collins Cox / Adam Cuerden, public domain); Rahul Dravid (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); Sachin Tendulkar (Bollywood Hungama, CC BY 3.0); Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Atomic Habits
shelf.creator: James Clear
shelf.why: The best book on pro­duc­tiv­ity Amit has read, and the one to start with if you read only one: turn your mind from goals to habits and pro­cesses, the com­pound in­ter­est of self-improvement, and use small re­wards to make habits stick.

shelf.title: Ali Abdaal’s YouTube channel
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Useful for fig­ur­ing out tools, men­tal mod­els and frame­works.

shelf.title: Thomas Frank’s YouTube channel
shelf.creator: Thomas Frank
shelf.why: Another cre­ator who started small and built him­self up by prac­tis­ing what he teaches.

shelf.title: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Advice Amit takes se­ri­ously be­cause it comes from some­one who has done it: make two videos a week for two years and don’t look at the num­bers, the an­ti­dote to quit­ting while you’re still bad.

shelf.title: How I Gained 1 MILLION Subscribers
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Ali Abdaal’s growth graph shows ex­po­nen­tial growth in prac­tice: al­most noth­ing for a long time (about 1,000 sub­scribers after 50 videos and half a year), then a near-vertical line.

shelf.title: The Parable of the Pottery Class
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: A short telling of the ex­per­i­ment where the group that made many pots beat the group that planned one per­fect pot.

shelf.title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children’s motivation and performance
shelf.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
shelf.why: The study be­hind Amit’s ad­vice to ‘focus on verbs, not adjectives’: chil­dren praised for being smart later tried less and even cheated, while chil­dren praised for ef­fort kept im­prov­ing.

shelf.title: How to Enhance Performance & Learning by Applying a Growth Mindset
shelf.creator: Huberman Lab Podcast
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great episode of a pod­cast that is ex­cel­lent on the whole.

shelf.title: Roam Research
shelf.why: Amit’s note-taking tool, which he calls a game changer: nested en­tries and two-way links turn any term into a hub of re­lated notes, re­plac­ing his scroll-and-search Word files and mak­ing up for a mem­ory he says isn’t great.

shelf.title: Notion
shelf.why: He thinks it’s a great pro­duc­tiv­ity tool, though he hasn’t re­ally started using it.

shelf.title: Obsidian
shelf.why: It is easy to run lo­cally on Linux and stores notes as plain Markdown files, so the whole Unix toolchain can work on them.

shelf.title: Building a Second Brain
shelf.creator: Tiago Forte
shelf.why: The brain is a messy, im­pres­sion­is­tic tool for re­tain­ing knowl­edge.

shelf.title: GNU Emacs
shelf.creator: Richard Stallman and James Gosling
shelf.why: Ajay’s ed­i­tor of choice: a fifty-year-old, fully pro­gram­mable tool whose age has pro­duced el­e­gant de­sign and bul­let­proof code.

shelf.title: Org Mode
shelf.why: It does much of what Amit de­moed in Roam and is very pow­er­ful.

shelf.title: Unix and the command line
shelf.why: After 40 years around com­put­ers, he con­sid­ers it the most pro­duc­tive and pow­er­ful en­vi­ron­ment there is.

shelf.title: TeX
shelf.creator: Donald Knuth
shelf.why: A pro­fes­sional type­set­ting sys­tem used for many great books.

shelf.title: Final Draft
shelf.why: The spe­cialised tool for writ­ing screen­plays.

shelf.title: Scrivener
shelf.why: The tool for writ­ing books, an­other of the sin­gle-purpose apps Amit has used.

shelf.title: Getting Things Done
shelf.creator: David Allen
shelf.why: Named as the clas­sic of the pro­duc­tiv­ity-tools-and-procedures tra­di­tion, which Ajay ques­tions as too man­age­rial.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral his­tory that Amit calls per­haps his most mem­o­rable, and the episode through which many lis­ten­ers find the show.

shelf.title: Abbé Faria: The Hypnotic Story of A Goan Son
shelf.creator: Carol Lobo
shelf.why: Background on the Goan prodigy who be­came one of the fa­thers of hyp­no­tism.

shelf.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
shelf.creator: Alexandre Dumas
shelf.why: It has a char­ac­ter named after Abbé Faria, which links the episode’s mantra to clas­sic lit­er­a­ture.

shelf.title: The BJP Before Modi (Episode 202, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Source of Sitapati’s line ‘Never let per­fec­tion be the enemy of production’.

shelf.title: Born a Muslim
shelf.creator: Ghazala Wahab
shelf.why: He points to her sen­tence about her grand­fa­ther shelling pine nuts all day to re­ward the chil­dren as a model of show­ing rather than telling.

shelf.title: Being Muslim in India (Episode 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s con­ver­sa­tion with Ghazala Wahab, which he holds up as a show­case of what his chap­ter-by-chapter note-taking pro­duces; her book also sup­plies a beau­ti­ful ex­am­ple of ‘show, don’t tell’.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Our Unlucky Children
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­kets give us forty flavours of potato chips and a thou­sand sham­poos while ed­u­ca­tion stays one-size-fits-all, built in the 19th cen­tury to pro­duce work­ers, be­cause mar­kets aren’t al­lowed to work there.

shelf.title: Doing better than a competitive exam
shelf.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Nitin Pai and Ajay’s case against or­gan­is­ing Indian ed­u­ca­tion around sin­gle exams like UPSC, IIT-JEE and the boards, with a pro­posal: a con­cep­tual exam to qual­ify the top one lakh stu­dents, then a lot­tery for IIT seats.

shelf.title: Song of Myself, 51
shelf.creator: Walt Whitman
shelf.why: The source of ‘we con­tain multitudes’, Amit’s ex­cuse for of­fer­ing ad­vice that con­tra­dicts it­self.

shelf.title: The God Delusion
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s case against or­gan­ised re­li­gion and dogma, which Amit thinks de­serves to be taken se­ri­ously even though his own athe­ism is gen­tler.

shelf.title: Episodes of The Seen and the Unseen with Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit calls him a bril­liant econ­o­mist doing amaz­ing work who is clearly on that track.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit on no one watch­ing you: ‘No one is tak­ing screen­shots and wait­ing to put it on Twitter to shame you, or ac­tu­ally in my case, they are.’
Ajay: ‘the prob­lem with prac­ti­cal goals is that you’ll ac­tu­ally achieve them.’ Amit: ‘It’s like the dog that chases a car and fi­nally catches it and whatcha gonna do then.’

After Ajay crit­i­cises aca­demics chas­ing ‘pubs’, Amit says: ‘it is not only aca­demics who want pubs. I was once in Europe, it was a hot sunny day, beer peena tha, main pub dhoondh raha tha’ (I wanted a beer, I was look­ing for a pub).
Amit after Ajay’s Unix trib­ute: ‘What does a Marathi pro­gram­mer say to an­other Marathi pro­gram­mer when he finds a flaw in a com­puter pro­gram? Bug, bug. So any­way, bug is Marathi for see.’
Ajay dis­likes the word pro­duc­tiv­ity be­cause ‘it’s too much of a man­age­rial thing. It’s too much Taylorism for me.’
